name: Additions to Daniel: Susanna
sourceNote: Translated from the Greek of Susanna in the version of Theodotion, as printed in H. B. Swete, *The Old Testament in Greek according to the Septuagint*, vol. 3 (1899; public domain), which also prints the Old Greek (Septuagint proper, preserved in full in the Chigi manuscript 88 and the Syro-Hexapla) on the facing page; differences of substance in the Old Greek are given in the notes. In Theodotion's manuscripts Susanna stands at the head of the book of Daniel, introducing Daniel as a youth; in the Old Greek and in the Latin Vulgate it follows Dan 12, and in the Vulgate and Catholic Bibles it is numbered Daniel 13 (verses 1–64 here match Dan 13:1–64). The Old Greek is shorter (it has nothing corresponding to verses 1–5a or the bath scene of 15–18 in the same form, and ends differently). The puns on tree names in verses 54–59 suggested to early readers (Julius Africanus, about AD 240, as reported) that the story was composed in Greek; others hold that an original Hebrew or Aramaic story was retold with new puns. Susanna is received as Scripture by Catholic and Orthodox churches; Protestant churches place it among the Apocrypha. Greek *kyrios* is rendered “Lord” and *theos* “God.” Dates are given as BC/AD. Readings not checked directly against the manuscripts are cited “as reported.” Brenton's English (1844), which translates the Old Greek, was consulted only as a check and not copied. CJT draft.

verses.text: There was a man living in Babylon, and his name was Joakim.{a}
And he took a wife whose name was Susanna,{b} daughter of Hilkiah, very beautiful and one who feared the Lord.
Her parents, too, were just people, and they had instructed their daughter in keeping with Moses' law.
Joakim was extremely wealthy, and next to his house he had a garden; the Jews regularly visited him, since he was the most respected of all of them.
And two elders from the people were appointed judges in that year, about whom the Master had spoken: “Lawlessness came out of Babylon, from elders who were judges, who seemed to guide the people.”{c}
These men spent much time in Joakim's house, and all who had cases to be judged would come to them there.
And when the people went away at midday, Susanna would go in and walk about in her husband's garden.
And the two elders watched her every day going in and walking about, and they came to be in lust for her.
And they twisted their own minds and turned their eyes away so as not to look to heaven or remember just judgments.
And both were pierced with desire for her, yet they did not disclose their pain to each other,
for they were ashamed to disclose their lust, that they wished to lie with her.
And they watched eagerly every day to see her.
They said to each other, “Let’s go home; it is time for lunch.” So they left and separated.

And turning back they came to the same place, and when they questioned each other about the reason, they owned up to their lust. And then together they fixed a time when they would be able to find her alone.

And it happened, while they were watching for a fit day, that she went in as on the day before and the day before that, with only two maidservants, and she wished to bathe in the garden, for it was hot.{d}
And there was no one there except the two elders, who had hidden and were watching her.
And she said to the maids, “Bring me olive oil and soap, and shut the doors of the garden, so that I may bathe.”
And they did just as she told them: they closed the garden doors, then slipped out through the side doors to fetch what she had asked for; and the elders they never saw, since these were in hiding.
And it happened, when the maids had gone out, that the two elders got up and ran to her and said,
“Look, the doors of the garden are shut, and no one sees us, and we are in desire for you; so agree with us and be with us.
But if not, we will testify against you that a young man was with you and that this is why you sent the maids away from you.”
Susanna groaned and said, “I am trapped on all sides. If I do this, it means my death; if I refuse, I will not get away from you.
Better that I refrain and fall into your hands than that I sin in the Lord's sight.”
Then Susanna shouted aloud, and the pair of elders shouted out against her as well.
And one of them ran and opened the doors of the garden.
And when those in the house heard the outcry in the garden, they rushed in by the side door to see what had happened to her.
And when the elders told their tale, the slaves were deeply ashamed, for never had such a word been spoken about Susanna.
And it happened on the next day, when the people gathered to her husband Joakim, that the two elders came, full of their lawless intent against Susanna, to have her put to death.
And they said before the people, “Send for Susanna, daughter of Hilkiah, who is Joakim's wife.” And they sent.
And she came, and her parents and her children and all her relatives.
Now Susanna was exceedingly delicate and beautiful in appearance.
And the lawless men ordered her to be unveiled, for she was veiled, so that they might take their fill of her beauty.
And those with her and all who saw her were weeping.
Then the pair of elders rose in the middle of the people and placed their hands on her head.{e}
But she, in tears, gazed up heavenward, because her heart had put its trust in the Lord.
And the elders said, “While we were walking about in the garden by ourselves, this woman came in with two maids, and she shut the doors of the garden and sent the maids away.
Then a youth, who was lying hidden there, approached her and lay with her.
And we were in a corner of the garden, and seeing the lawlessness we ran to them;
and though we saw the two of them together, we could not hold him, since he was stronger than we were; he opened the doors and sprang out.
But we seized this woman and questioned her as to who the young man was,
and she refused to tell us. This is our testimony.” Because they were elders and judges of the people, the assembly believed them and sentenced her to death.
And Susanna cried out with a loud voice and said, “God of the age, who knows hidden things, who knows all things before they come to be,
you know that they have testified falsely against me. And see, I am dying, though I have done none of the things that these men have wickedly made up against me.”
And the Lord heard her voice.
And as she was being led away to be destroyed, God stirred up the holy spirit of a young boy whose name was Daniel,{f}
and he shouted with a loud voice, “I am clean of the blood of this woman!”
Then the whole people swung round toward him and said, “What is this you have just said?”
And he, standing in their midst, said, “Are you such fools, sons of Israel? Without examining and without learning the plain truth, have you condemned a daughter of Israel?
Go back to the place of judgment, for these men have testified falsely against her.”
So the whole people hurried back. And the elders said to him, “Come, take your seat in our midst and make it known to us, since God has granted you the rank of an elder.”
Daniel said to them, “Set the two a good distance apart, one from the other, and I will put them to the question.”
And when they had been separated one from the other, he called one of them and said to him, “You who have grown old in days of evil, now your sins have come home, which you committed before,
judging unjust judgments, condemning the innocent and letting the guilty go free, though the Lord says, ‘The innocent and the righteous you shall not kill.’{g}
Now then, if you really saw her, tell me: under what tree did you see them having intercourse with each other?” And he said, “Under a mastic tree.”{h}
And Daniel said, “Well have you lied against your own head; for already the angel of God has received the sentence from God and will split you in two.”
And putting him aside, he ordered them to bring the other, and said to him, “Offspring of Canaan and not of Judah, beauty has deceived you, and desire has twisted your heart.
This is how you were dealing with the daughters of Israel, and they were having intercourse with you out of fear; but a daughter of Judah would not endure your lawlessness.
Now tell me: beneath which tree did you see them having sex?” He answered, “Under an evergreen oak.”{i}
And Daniel said to him, “Well have you too lied against your own head; for the angel of God is waiting with the sword to saw you in two, so as to destroy you both.”
And the whole assembly cried out with a loud voice and blessed God, who saves those who hope in him.

And they rose up against the two elders, because Daniel had convicted them out of their own mouth of having testified falsely, and they did to them just as they had wickedly planned to do to their neighbor;
acting according to the law of Moses,{j} they killed them. And innocent blood was saved on that day.
And Hilkiah and his wife gave praise for their daughter, with Joakim her husband and all her relatives, because nothing shameful was found in her.
And Daniel became great before the people from that day onward.{k}

notes.text: In the Latin Vulgate and Catholic Bibles this book is Daniel 13. Verses 1–5a are lacking in the Old Greek, which begins abruptly with the elders.
The saying is not found in the Old Testament; some compare Jer 29:20–23, where two false prophets in Babylon, Ahab and Zedekiah, are condemned for adultery.
Verses 15–18 have no counterpart in the Old Greek, which tells the story without the bath.
The Old Greek, as reported, reads instead that “an angel of the Lord gave a spirit of understanding to a young man,” Daniel.

Greek schinos, the mastic or lentisk, a small evergreen shrub. Daniel answers with a pun: schinos / schisei, “will split.” An English imitation would be “under a clove tree … the angel will cleave you.”
Greek prinos, the holm oak (Quercus ilex). The pun is prinos / prisai, “to saw.” An English imitation would be “under a yew … to hew you.”
Deut 19:16–21. The Old Greek, as reported, says that they gagged them, led them out, and threw them into a ravine, and that the angel of the Lord cast fire between them.
The Old Greek ends instead with praise of the young: “For this reason the young are beloved of Jacob for their simplicity…,” as reported.
